Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verses 1–2:

Makkiyya except verses 68, 69 and 70, which are Madaniyya; its verses number 77. [It was revealed after Ya-Sin.] In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful.

Al-barakah (blessing): abundance of good and its increase. From it comes (Tabaraka Allah) ("Blessed is Allah"), and in it there are two meanings: the increase of His good, and its multiplicity.

Or: He has increased beyond everything and is exalted above it in His attributes and His acts. Al-Furqan is a verbal noun from faraqa between two things, meaning when he separated them. It was named the Qur'an because it separates (fasl) between truth and falsehood. Or because it was not sent down all at once, but in separated portions, divided between one part and another in the sending down. [Mahmud said: "It is permissible that his description as al-Furqan refers to his distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and it is permissible that it refers to his being sent down in portions, bit by bit, as He said: 'And a Qur'an We have divided (faraqnahu) that you might recite it to the people at intervals.'" Ahmad said: The more evident meaning here is the second, because in the course of the surah, after the verses (And they say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"), Allah the Exalted said (Thus) — that is, We sent it down in portions in this way — (so that We may strengthen your heart by it). So describing it as al-Furqan at the beginning of the surah — and Allah knows best — is like a preface and introduction to what comes after.]. Do you not see His saying (And a Qur'an We have divided, that you might recite it to the people at intervals, and We have sent it down in stages)? The word al-farq has also come with this same meaning. [His saying "al-farq has also come with this meaning": in al-Sihah: "al-Farq also: al-furqan. Its counterpart is al-khusr and al-khusran." The rajiz said: "And a polytheist..." etc. (ʿ).] He said:

"And a polytheist, disbelieving in the al-Furq"

From Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him: "upon His servants," and they are the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Ummah, as He said (We have sent down to you) and (Say: "We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us"). The pronoun in (li-yakuna) refers either to His servant or to al-Furqan.

What supports its referring to al-Furqan is Ibn al-Zubayr's reading li-l-ʿalamina for the jinn and mankind: nadhiran, meaning warning, or a warning (indhar), like al-nakir in the sense of al-inkar. From it is His saying (So how was My punishment and warning?).

(Alladhi lahu) is in the nominative case, either as a substitution (ibdal) for (alladhi nazzala), or as nominative by way of praise, or it is in the accusative on that basis. If you ask: how is it permissible to separate the substitute from what it substitutes? I say: it is not separated by anything, because the element substituted has its relative clause "nazzala". And (li-yakuna) is a causal clause for it, as if the substituted element were not complete except by it.

If you ask: in creation (al-khalq) there is the meaning of measuring, so what is the meaning of His saying (And He created everything and measured it with precise measure)? As if He said: "He created everything and measured everything"? I say: the meaning is that He brought into being every thing in a creation that observes measure and proportion, so He measured it and made it ready for what suits it. An example: He created the human being in this measured, proportioned form which you see, measuring him for the duties and interests assigned to him in the matters of religion and the world. Likewise every animal and inanimate thing He brought forth in a disposition that is balanced and measured, with the examples of wisdom and management, so He measured it for some matter and some benefit, corresponding to what it was measured for, without deviating from it. Or, Allah's bringing into being is called creation (khalq), because He does not bring anything into being for His wisdom except in a manner of measure without disparity; so when it is said "Allah created such-and-such," it is like your saying "He produced and brought into existence," without regard to the derivational sense. It is as if it were said: "He brought every thing into existence and measured it, in its bringing into existence, not bringing it into existence in disparity." It has also been said: "so He made for it a limit and an end," meaning: He measured it for remaining until a known term.

Al-Khalq in the sense of al-if'tiʿal (fabrication, making), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols, and you invent a lie﴾ [29:17]. The meaning is: they preferred to the worship of Allah, glory be to Him, the worship of gods that are the most evidently powerless of all things, who are unable to do anything of the acts of Allah or of the acts of the servants, since they do not create anything, whereas they themselves are created, because their worshippers make them by carving and shaping. ﴿And they have no power﴾, meaning: they are unable to ward off harm from themselves or bring benefit to themselves, whereas they (the worshippers) are able to do so. And if they are powerless to create and to ward off harm and bring benefit, which are within the capacity of servants, then they are even more powerless with regard to death, life and resurrection, which no one can do except Allah.

**Qawmun ākharūn** (other people). It was said: they are the Jews. And it was said: ʿAddās, the freedman of Ḥuwaiṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā; Yasār, the freedman of al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī; and Abū Fukayha al-Rūmī. This was said by al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Dār.

"Jāʾa" and "atā" are used in the sense of a verb, so they take the same complement (*taʿdiya*) as that verb, and it may be understood in the sense of "they came to" with injustice (*ẓulman*), as you say: "I came to the place" (*jiʾtu al-makān*). It is permissible to delete the preposition and let the verb connect directly to its object.

Their injustice (*ẓulmuhum*) was that they made an Arab learn from a non-Arab Roman a speech in Arabic that, by its eloquence, rendered all the eloquent Arabs unable to match it. And the false speech (*al-zūr*) was that they slandered him by attributing to him what he was innocent of.

Asatir al-Awwalin (the tales of the ancients): what the earlier people wrote down, such as the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar. It is a plural of ustur or usturah, like uhdutha (a tale, a story). Iktatabaha: he wrote them down for himself and took them, just as you say: istakabba al-ma' wa-istabbahu, when he poured it out and poured it for himself and took it.

It is also read as uktutibat, in the passive form. The meaning is: a scribe wrote them for him, because he was illiterate and could not write with his own hand, and this is part of the completeness of his miracle. Then the preposition (lam) was dropped, so the verb reached the pronoun and became iktatabaha iyyahu katib, like His saying (and Musa chose his people). Then the verb was built for the pronoun which is iyyahu, so it changed into a hidden nominative after having been an explicit accusative, and the pronoun of the tales remained as it was, so it became (iktatabaha), as you see.

If you say: how is it said iktatabaha, when fa-hiya tumla alayhi (then they are dictated to him) is what is said, since one says amlaytu alayhi fa-huwa yaktatibuha (I dictated to him, so he writes them)? I say: there are two possibilities. One: he intended iktitabuha or requesting them, so they are dictated to him. Or: they were written for him while he was illiterate, so they are dictated to him, meaning: they are cast upon him from his writing, he memorizes them, because the image of casting upon the memorizer is the same as the image of casting upon the scribe.

From al-Hasan: it is God's own saying, refuting them. It would only be correct if the hamza were opened as an interrogative with the meaning of denial. Its manner would be like his saying:

Afrahu an arza'a al-kiram wa-an … awarritha dhawdan shasa'isa nablan
In compare: in carrying out the killing of the generous, and that I inherit a herd of she-camels, scrawny and little-milked…

[The verse is attributed to Hadrami ibn Amir, addressing Juz ibn Sinan ibn Mu'allah when he accused him of rejoicing at taking the blood-money for his slain brother. It is also said to be by Jarir, but that is not right. Juz (with fatha then sukun) — and in, here, is conditional, unattached to the particle of negation, or in the sense of idh (when). Azantani: i.e., you accused me of it.

That is: with that vile deed, falsely, O Juz, so it is a vocative; then may you meet a quick death after it: a curse upon him that he receives the same swiftly, so that he may see whether he will rejoice or grieve. It is narrated: "then you meet its like quickly." Afrahu, i.e., "Should I rejoice that I suffer the loss of the generous ones and strike among them?" The interrogative hamza of denial or wonder has been dropped on the assumption of its occurrence, as the context indicates it, and so the speech is presented in the form of assertion and affirmation, so that the opponent's claim's ugliness becomes evident. Arza'a is passive, and so is awurritha, meaning: he is given a herd, i.e., a group of camels, after their death. Al-dhawd: what is between three and ten, a feminine noun with no singular from its own form; it is used here to express the whole blood-money, as belittling it. Therefore he described it as shasa'isa, the plural of shasus, which is a she-camel of little milk. Its ending was changed for the metre. Al-nabl (with kasra, like sabab) is the plural of nabil; it is also narrated with a damma, so it is also a plural of nabil, like karm and karim, or a plural of nablah, like ghurf and ghurfah.

That is: the small ones? Or the noble ones? It is then one of the words with opposite meanings, but the first is more suitable to the context. It is permissible that the blood-money was ten.]

It is right for al-Hasan to stop at "al-awwalin."

Bukratan wa-asilan: i.e., continually, or in secret before people spread out, and when they return to their dwellings.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 6:

That is, He knows every hidden secret in the heavens and the earth. Among what He knows is what you conceal of plotting against His Messenger (ﷺ), though you know that what you say is falsehood and lies. Likewise, He knows the inner reality of the affair of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his innocence of what you slander him with. He will repay you and repay him for what He knows of you and what He knows of him.

If you ask: How does His saying ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ correspond to this meaning? I answer: Since what preceded it was in the sense of a threat, He followed it with something that indicates the power to carry it out, for one is not described as forgiving and merciful except one who is able to punish. Or it is a reminder that by this obstinacy of theirs they deserved that the punishment be poured down upon them in full, but that He has turned it away from them: He is Forgiving and Merciful, granting respite and not hastening.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 7–8:

The lam [in the word "rasul" as written in some copies] appears in the Mushaf separated from this [word] and outside the conventions of Arabic script. The orthography of the Mushaf is a sunnah that does not change. In this there is a dismissal and a belittling of its (the Prophet's) status, and calling him "messenger" is mockery and derision from them (qawluhu "wa-tanz" in al-Sihah: "al-tanz" is mockery (al-sukhriyya). (ʿ))—as if they were saying: "What is this claimant that he is a messenger?" A similar statement is the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾. That is: if it is true that he is the messenger of God, then what is the matter with him, that his state is like our state: ﴿he eats food as we eat, and walks in the markets seeking a livelihood as we walk﴾. They mean that he should have been an angel, free of need for eating and for earning a living. Then they descended from their proposal that he be an angel to the proposal that he be a human with an angel accompanying him, so that the two might support each other in warning and admonition. Then they descended again and said: even if he is not supported by an angel, let him be supported by a treasure cast down to him from heaven, by which he may be strengthened and not need to seek his livelihood. Then they descended further and were content that he be a man who has a garden from which he eats and earns his provision, as the landowners and the wealthy do. Or they (the disbelievers) would eat from that garden and benefit from it in their worldly life and livelihood. By "the wrongdoers" he meant precisely them: the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to record their wrongdoing in what they said. It was also read: ﴿fa-yakūnu﴾ with a raised (ḍamma) vowel, or ﴿aw yakūnu lahu jannah﴾ with the yāʾ, and ﴿nakulu﴾ with the nūn. If you ask: what are the grounds for the raising and the accusative in ﴿fa-yakūnu﴾? I say: the accusative is because it is the answer to "lawlā" in the sense of "halla," and its ruling is the ruling of the interrogative. The raising is on the basis that it is conjoined to "unzila," and its position is the nominative. Do you not see that you say "lawlā yunzalu" with the raising, and it is conjoined to it: "yulqā," and "takūnu," both in the nominative, and they cannot be in the accusative, because they are in the position of what occurs after "lawlā," and it can only be in the nominative. The speakers are the disbelieving Quraysh: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and those who joined them. ﴿Mashūran﴾: bewitched, whose intellect has been overcome by sorcery; or "dhū siḥr," meaning having a lung (riʾa). They meant that he is a human being and not an angel.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 10:

Takāthur (abundance) of good: ﴿He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾, namely [in] this world, ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, and will give you palaces﴾, which is to say He will hasten for you the like of what He has promised you in the Hereafter of gardens and palaces.

It is also read "wa-yajʿalu" (and He will make), with the nominative, in coordination with "jaʿala" (He has made), because when the conditional particle is followed by a past-tense verb, its response may be either jussive or nominative, as in the verse:

"And if a friend comes to him on the day of request, he says: 'Neither my wealth nor my family is absent.'" [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in the first volume, page 537, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector (muṣaḥḥiḥ).]]

In "wa-yajʿalu laka" (and He will make for you), when it is assimilated (idghām), the lām may be considered as both jussive and nominative. It is also read with the accusative, as a response to the conditional introduced by the waw.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verses 11–14:**

Bal kadhdhabu (﴿بَلْ كَذَّبُوا﴾, "Nay, they denied") is a conjunction (ʿatf) linking to what was reported about them. He says: "Nay, they came with something more astonishing than all of that, which is their denial of the Hour." It is also permissible for it to connect to what follows it, as if He said: "Nay, they denied the Hour, so how would they turn to this answer, and how would they believe in the hastening of something like what was promised to you in the Hereafter, when they do not believe in the Hereafter?"

Al-Sa'ir (﴿السَّعِيرَ﴾, "the Blaze"): the intensely blazing fire. It is reported from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is one of the names of Hell.

Ra'athhum (﴿رَأَتْهُمْ﴾, "saw them") is from their saying: "Their houses see each other (tatarra)," meaning they face each other. Mahmud said: "It comes from their saying: 'The houses of the sons of so-and-so face each other (tatarra),' figuratively." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: "There is no need to take it figuratively, for the seeing of Hell is possible, the power of Allah the Exalted is sufficient, and the apparent texts have converged on the occurrence of this possible matter and on Allah the Exalted creating for it sensory and intellectual perception. Do you not see His saying ﴿سَمِعُوا لَهَا تَغَيُّظًا﴾, and its dispute with Paradise, and its saying ﴿هَلْ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ﴾, and its complaint to its Lord, so that it was permitted two breaths, and other apparent texts for which there is no way to interpret them away, since there is no need for it. And if the door of interpretation and figurative language were opened in the matters of the Resurrection, the one who followed that would be tossed into the valley of misguidance and bewilderment, into the sects of the philosophers. So the truth is that we are bound to the apparent meaning as long as no obstacle prevents it, and Allah knows best."

That is, "and they will argue (tatanazaru)." And from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "Their fires should not see each other" (lā tarāʾā nārāhumā), mentioned earlier in al-Ma'idah, it is as if one of them sees the other figuratively.

The meaning: when it is in their sight from a distance, they hear the sound of its boiling. This is compared to the sound of one who is enraged and exhaling heavily (al-zafir). It is also permissible that the meaning be: when its guardians (zabaniyah) see them, they become enraged and exhale heavily in anger at the disbelievers and in desire to take vengeance on them.

Al-Kurb (﴿الكَرْبِ﴾, "distress") comes with constriction, just as ease (al-rawh) comes with spaciousness. For this reason Allah described Paradise as having a width of "the heavens and the earth." It has come in the hadiths that every believer has such-and-such palaces and gardens. Allah has combined on the people of the Fire all kinds of constriction and oppression, placing them in a narrow place where they are pressed tightly together, as is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in his tafsir, that it is constricted upon them as the zajj (the metal butt) of a spear is constricted within it. And with that constriction, they are shackled and bound in chains.

﴿قُرِّنَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ إِلَى أَعْنَاقِهِمْ فِي الْجَوَامِعِ﴾ ("Their hands were bound to their necks in the collars"). It is said: each disbeliever will be bound together with his devil in one chain. And ﴿وَفِي أَرْجُلِهِمُ الْأَصْفَادُ﴾ ("and in their feet are the shackles").

Al-Thubur (﴿ثُبُورًا﴾, "destruction") means ruin. Their calling for it is that it be said: "Woe to us (wa thubūrāh)!" meaning: "Come, O destruction, for this is your time and your moment." ﴿لَا تَدْعُوا﴾ ("Do not call") means it is said to them, or they are more worthy that it be said to them, even if there is no actual speech. And the meaning of ﴿وَادْعُوا ثُبُورًا كَثِيرًا﴾ ("but call for much destruction") is that you have fallen into something whose destruction is not single, but is rather manifold, either because the punishment has many kinds and varieties, each kind being a destruction in its severity and horror, or because whenever their skins are roasted through, they are replaced with other skins, so there is no end to their ruin.

When the angels and the messengers clear themselves from the attribution of misguidance, which is the work of the devils, and seek refuge from it, they are far more clear of it and exalt their Lord, the Self-Sufficient, the Just. They exalted Him when they attributed to Him the bounty of blessing and the enjoyment of it, and ascribed the forgetting of the Remembrance and the cause of perdition to the unbelievers. They thus explained the metaphorical misguidance which God ascribed to His own Essence in His saying 'He leads astray whom He wills.' Had He been the misguider in reality, the ready answer would have been: 'Rather, You led them astray.' The meaning: 'Did you cause them to fall into error from the path of truth, or did they themselves stray from it?' Ḍalla is the intransitive of aḍalla, and the analogy would be ḍalla ʿan al-sabīl, but they dropped the preposition as they dropped it in hadāhu al-ṭarīq. The original is ilā al-ṭarīq and li-l-ṭarīq. Their saying aḍalla al-baʿīr means: made it lost (ḍāllan), i.e., wasted; since most of that happens through the owner's negligence and lack of care in guarding it, it is said aḍallahu, whether or not any act was done by him. Subḥānaka: an expression of wonder at them; they marvelled at what was said to them, since they are angels and prophets, infallible, so how far are they from the misguiding which is specific to Iblis and his party.

Or they uttered Subḥānaka to show that they are the glorifiers, the sanctified, marked with that, so how could it befit their state that they should lead His servants astray. Or they intended by it His exaltation above rivals, that any prophet, angel or other should be a rival to Him; then they said: 'It is not right nor proper for us, being infallible, that we should take any protector apart from You. How could it be right for us to make others take us as protectors apart from You?' Or: 'It was not fitting for us to be like the devils in their befriending of the unbelievers, as the unbelievers befriended them.' God, exalted, said: 'So fight the friends of Satan' (4:76), meaning the unbelievers, and He said: 'And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Ṭāghūt' (2:257). The indefiniteness of awliyāʾ is because they are particular protectors, namely the jinn and idols. Al-dhikr: the remembrance of God and belief in Him, or the Qur'an and the laws. Al-bawr: ruin, which is applied to the singular and the plural; it may be the plural of bāʾir, like ʿāʾidh and ʿawdh."

They thus explained the metaphorical misguidance which God ascribed to His own Essence in His saying 'He leads astray whom He wills.' Had He been the misguider in reality, the ready answer would have been: 'Rather, You led them astray.' The meaning: 'Did you cause them to fall into error from the path of truth, or did they themselves stray from it?' Ḍalla is the intransitive of aḍalla, and the analogy would be ḍalla ʿan al-sabīl, but they dropped the preposition as they dropped it in hadāhu al-ṭarīq. The original is ilā al-ṭarīq and li-l-ṭarīq. Their saying aḍalla al-baʿīr means: made it lost (ḍāllan), i.e., wasted; since most of that happens through the owner's negligence and lack of care in guarding it, it is said aḍallahu, whether or not any act was done by him. Subḥānaka: an expression of wonder at them; they marvelled at what was said to them, since they are angels and prophets, infallible, so how far are they from the misguiding which is specific to Iblis and his party.

Or they uttered Subḥānaka to show that they are the glorifiers, the sanctified, marked with that, so how could it befit their state that they should lead His servants astray. Or they intended by it His exaltation above rivals, that any prophet, angel or other should be a rival to Him; then they said: 'It is not right nor proper for us, being infallible, that we should take any protector apart from You. How could it be right for us to make others take us as protectors apart from You?' Or: 'It was not fitting for us to be like the devils in their befriending of the unbelievers, as the unbelievers befriended them.' God, exalted, said: 'So fight the friends of Satan' (4:76), meaning the unbelievers, and He said: 'And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Ṭāghūt' (2:257). Abū Jaʿfar al-Madanī read natakhidha (we take) in the passive form. This verb, ittakhadha, is transitive to one object, as in ittakhadha waliyyan, and to two, as in ittakhadha fulanan waliyyan. God, exalted, said: 'Or have they taken gods from the earth?' (21:21) and 'And God took Abraham as a close friend' (4:125). The first reading is from the verb transitive to one object, which is min awliyāʾ, the original being: that we take protectors; min was added to stress the negation. The second is from the verb transitive to two objects: the first is what the verb was built for, and the second is min awliyāʾ. Min is partitive, meaning: we do not take some of the protectors. The indefiniteness of awliyāʾ is because they are particular protectors, namely the jinn and idols. Al-dhikr: the remembrance of God and belief in Him, or the Qur'an and the laws. Al-bawr: ruin, which is applied to the singular and the plural; it may be the plural of bāʾir, like ʿāʾidh and ʿawdh."

This surprise [[His saying "this surprise," i.e., the one in His saying, "Then they have indeed denied you."(ʿ)]] in argument and reproach is excellent and striking, especially when it is combined with *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person) and the omission of the verb of saying (*ḥadhf al-qawl*), and similar devices. An example is His saying, ﴿O People of the Scripture, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you after a gap in the messengers, lest you say, "No bearer of good tidings and no warner has come to us." Indeed, a bearer of good tidings and a warner has come to you﴾ (5:19). And the saying of the poet:

*They said, "Khurasan is the farthest that we are to be taken, then the return,"*
*But we have already come to Khurasan.*

[[He means: they said that this city is the farthest point to which we are to be taken and the furthest extent of our journey, and then there is the return, i.e., the coming back. It is also permissible that "the return" is a conjunction with "Khurasan." His saying, "But we have already come," is connected to an omitted element, meaning: if they are truthful in their saying, "We have already come to Khurasan," then why have we not been freed from the journey? It is also permissible that he shifts to the second person, meaning: so say to them, "Cut the journey short with us and return, for we have already reached the destination." But that is not *iltifat*.]]

It is also recited as *yaqūlūna* with both the *tā'* and the *yā'*. The one who reads with the *tā'* means: "Then they have denied you by your saying that they are gods." The one who reads with the *yā'* means: "Then they have denied you by their saying, ﴿Glory be to You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ (25:18)."

If you say: Does the function of the *bā'* differ between the *tā'* and the *yā'*? I say: Yes, by God. With the *tā'*, it is like His saying, ﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾ (50:5), and the prepositional phrase is a substitute for the pronoun, as if it were said: "Then they have denied what you say." With the *yā'*, it is like your saying, "I wrote with the pen."

It is also recited as *yastaṭīʿūna* with both the *tā'* and the *yā'*. That is: "Will you, O disbelievers, be able to turn away the punishment from yourselves?" It was also said that *al-ṣarf* means repentance, and it was said that it means cunning, from their saying, "He is indeed *yatasarraf*," i.e., he devises a stratagem. Or the meaning is: "Will your gods be able to turn away the punishment from you, or to devise a stratagem for you?"

The address is general, to all who are responsible (*mukallafūn*). The great punishment befalls everyone who wrongs, and the disbeliever is a wrongdoer, according to His saying, ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a tremendous wrong﴾ (31:13), and the sinner is a wrongdoer, according to His saying, ﴿And whoever does not repent, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ (49:11).

It is also recited as *yudhqhu* with the *yā'*, and in it the pronoun refers to God, or it refers to the verbal noun of *yaẓlim*.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 20:

The clause after "illa" (except) is a qualifier (sifa) of an omitted noun. The meaning is: "And We did not send before you any of the messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets." The noun was omitted because the prepositional phrase ("from among the messengers") is sufficient to indicate it. Similar to this is the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾, meaning: "And there is none of us but [there is an individual who has a known station]." It has also been read as "yamshuna" (they walk), in the passive form, meaning: "their needs cause them to walk," or "people cause them to walk." If it were read as "yamshuna" (active), it would be more appropriate, were it not for the transmitted reading. It has also been said: this is an argument against those who said, ﴿What is this Messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾

"Fitnah" means a trial and a test. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what they said and considered strange, namely his eating food and walking in the markets, after He had argued against them with all the other messengers. He says: "It is My custom and the demand of My wisdom to test some of you, O people, by means of others." The meaning is that He tested the messengers through those to whom they were sent, through their hostility toward them, their statements that went beyond the bounds of fairness, the various kinds of their harm, and He asked them for patient endurance, similar to ﴿You will certainly hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed among the steadfast matters﴾. The placement of "atasbirun" (will you be patient?) after mention of the trial corresponds to the placement of "ayyukum" (which of you) after the test in His saying ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. "Basira" means knowing what is right regarding what He tests with and other matters, so do not let your breast be constricted, nor let their statements provoke you lightly, for in your patience with them lies your happiness and success in both abodes. It has also been said: this is a consolation to him for what they reproached him with, namely poverty, when they said: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him, or a treasure not been thrown to him, or he not been given a garden?﴾ And that He made the rich a trial for the poor, to see whether they would be patient; and that this is His wisdom and His will: He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. It has also been said: We made you a trial for them, for if you were rich, a possessor of treasures and gardens, their inclination toward you and their obedience to you would be for worldly gain, or mixed with worldly gain; so We sent you poor, so that the obedience of those who obey you would be purely for the sake of God's countenance, without worldly greed. It has also been said: Abu Jahl, al-Walidayn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, and those of their rank used to say: "If we embrace Islam after Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal, and so-and-so and so-and-so, who embraced it before us, they will rise above us through presumption based on precedence." So this is the trial of some of them by means of others.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 21:

That is: they do not hope for our meeting with good, because they are disbelievers. Or: they do not fear our meeting with evil. In the dialect of Tihama, "rajaʾ" (hope) means "khawf" (fear), and on this basis is explained His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from Allah?﴾ [71:13]. He made the arrival at the abode of His recompense equivalent to meeting Him, were it the case that one would meet Him.

They proposed, among the signs, that Allah send down the angels to them to inform them that Muhammad is truthful, so that they would believe him. Or that they see Allah openly, so that He would command them to believe in him and follow him. There is no escape from one of two possibilities: either they knew that Allah does not send angels to anyone other than the prophets, and that Allah cannot be seen [[His saying "cannot be seen": this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila; according to the People of the Sunna, He can be seen (ʿ).]], and so they conditioned their faith on something that would not occur; or they did not know this, and they only intended obstinacy by proposing signs other than the signs that had already come down and by which the proof had been established against them, as the people of Moses did when they said: "We will not believe you until we see Allah openly."

If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿in their souls﴾? I say: its meaning is that they concealed in their hearts arrogance toward the truth, which is disbelief and obstinacy, and they believed it, as He said: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride, which they will never attain.﴾ [40:56]. And ﴿they committed excess﴾: they exceeded the limit in wrongdoing. It is said: "So-and-so committed excess against us" (ʿatā ʿalaynā fulān). And the excess has been described as great, and he exaggerated in its extremity, meaning that they did not speak this grave utterance except because they had reached the utmost of arrogance and the farthest limit of transgression. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath. This sentence, in the goodness of its being introduced as a fresh statement, is at its peak. In its style is the saying of the poet:

"And the neighbour of Jassas, we equaled with her she-camel's tooth, Kulayb — how exalted was the tooth of Kulayb's equal!"

[[Said by a man of the Banu Bakr, boasting over the Banu Taghlib: the tribe of Jassas; Kulayb ibn Rabiʿa was the brother of Muhalhil and the maternal uncle of Imru' al-Qays. "Neighbour of Jassas" is his maternal aunt al-Basus. "Abana" (with hamza): we matched and equated Kulayb with her, "with her tooth," i.e., with her aged she-camel, and so we killed him over it. Then he said in wonder and amazement: "ghalat," i.e., rose and became great. An aged, emaciated she-camel; "bawwa'uha" Kulayb, the famous one.

"Bawaʾ" is like "sawaʾ" in measure and meaning, i.e., its equal and match is Kulayb ibn Rabiʿa, the well-known brave man. Among its story: al-Basus came with a man of Jarm to visit her sister Hayla, mother of Jassas ibn Murra. The Jarmi's she-camel went out grazing with the camels of the Banu Bakr in the land of Taghlib, because of the in-law relationship and affection between them. Kulayb denied the she-camel and thought it was foreign, so he shot it with an arrow which struck its udder, and it returned bleeding, and knelt in the courtyard of Jassas. Al-Basus saw it and cried: "Woe to my humiliation! Woe to my strangeness!" Jassas said: "Be calm; by Allah, I will hamstring a stallion among them which is dearer to its people than she is." Kulayb thought he meant a stallion he had named ʿAlyan, so he said: "Beyond ʿAlyan is the pulling of thorn-bush." But Jassas meant Kulayb himself. He lay in wait for him one day and struck him with his spear and felled him. ʿAmr ibn al-Harith followed him, and when Kulayb saw him he said to him:

"Give me water, O ʿAmr!" He said: "You left the water behind you," and he finished him off. Thus the famous proverb was coined:

"The one who seeks refuge with ʿAmr in his distress is like one who seeks refuge from scorched sand in fire."

The war between Bakr and Taghlib blazed for about thirty years, and the proverb spread: "Kulayb's blood-price for the she-camel" (sadda Kulayb fi al-nāqa).]]

In the implication of this act there is evidence of wonder without the wording of wonder. Do you not see that the meaning is: How great is their arrogance, how immense is their excess, and how exalted is the tooth whose equal is Kulayb?

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 22:**

﴿يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَ الْمَلَائِكَةَ﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) by one of two things. Either it is governed by what is implied by ﴿لَا بُشْرَىٰ﴾, meaning: on the day they see the angels, good tidings are prevented for them, or they are deprived of them. Or it is governed by an implied "remember" (uḍmār "udhkur"), meaning: remember the day they see the angels; then He said, ﴿لَا بُشْرَىٰ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾. And ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ is for repetition (al-takrīr).

As for ﴿لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾, it is either an apparent noun standing in the place of a pronoun, or it is general, so its generality encompasses them. ﴿حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا﴾ was mentioned by Sibawayh in the chapter on verbal nouns that are non-derivable (al-maṣādir ghayr al-mutaṣarrifa, i.e. verbal nouns that do not undergo inflectional variation), which are in the accusative governed by verbs whose appearance is omitted, such as: *ma'ādh Allāh* (God forbid), *qa'dak Allāh* (by God, your companion), and *'umrak Allāh* (by your life, God).

[[The words "qa'dak Allāh" are in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "Their saying: *qa'īduka lā ātīka*, and *qa'īduka Allāh lā ātīka*, and *qa'daka Allāh lā ātīka*" is an oath of the Arabs. These are verbal nouns used in the accusative with an implied verb. The meaning: by your companion who is the companion of every secret conversation, as one says: "I beseech you by God" (nashadtuka Allāh). (ʿ)]]

This is a phrase they used when meeting a hated enemy who had taken revenge, or when a calamity descended, or the like; they placed it in the position of seeking refuge. Sibawayh said: a man says to another, "Will you do such and such?" and he replies, "Ḥijran," and it comes from *ḥajarahu*, when he prevented him, because the one seeking refuge asks God to prevent the harm so that it does not reach him. So the meaning was: I ask God to prevent that, preventing it and enclosing it with a barrier (yaḥjuruhu ḥajran).

Its being in the pattern *fiʿl* or *fiʿl* in the reading of al-Ḥasan is an inflectional variation, because it is restricted to one position, just as *qa'dak* and *'umrak* were like that. I have cited a verse by one of the rajaz poets:

*Qālat wa-fīhā ḥaydatun wa-dhaʿr… ʿawdhu bi-rabbī minkum wa-ḥajr*
She said, while in her was aversion and terror: "I seek refuge in my Lord from you, and a barrier!"

[[*al-ḥaydah*: aversion, turning away; *dhaʿarahu dhaʿran*: he frightened him. *al-dhaʿr* with a *ḍamma* is a noun of verbal action; likewise *al-ʿawdh* means seeking refuge and taking shelter, and *al-ḥajr* means refusal and fortification. The subject is omitted, meaning: "her matter": she seeks refuge from you and fortifies herself with my Lord, while she is averse and terrified. This is said on their tongues when meeting something hateful.]]

If you say: since it is established that it is among the verbal nouns, what is the meaning of describing it as *maḥjūr*? I say: this description came to emphasise the meaning of *ḥajr*, as they said: *dhayl dhā'il* (abject humiliation), and *dhayl* means humiliation; and *mawt māʾit* (a dying death). The meaning in the verse is: they ask for the descent of the angels and demand it, but when they see them at death or on the Day of Resurrection, they dislike meeting them and are terrified of them, because they meet them only with what they dislike. They say upon seeing them what they used to say upon meeting a hated enemy who has taken revenge [[The word "al-mawtūr" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: the one whose slain was killed and who did not obtain blood-revenge for him. (ʿ)]] and a severe calamity.

It was also said: this is from the speech of the angels, and its meaning is: forbidden, prohibited for you are forgiveness, Paradise and good tidings; that is, God has made that forbidden for you.

Not here is there any arrival or anything resembling arrival. Rather, the state of those people and the deeds they performed in their disbelief, such as maintaining ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, showing kindness to a captive, and other of their noble and good qualities, are depicted as the state of a people who opposed their ruler and defied him. So he advanced upon their possessions and targeted what was under their control, ruining it and tearing it to every shred, leaving behind no trace of it and no dust [[His saying "leaving behind no trace of it and no dust" — in al-Sihah, "al-'athir" with a sukun on the tha' means dust. (ʿA)]]. And al-habaʾ (the floating mote): what comes out through a window together with the sunlight, resembling dust. In their proverbs: "Less than the scattered habaʾ." Mansuran (scattered) is an adjective of al-habaʾ. He likened them to the habaʾ in its scarcity and insignificance in his sight, and that it brings no benefit; then he likened them to its scattered part, because you see it ordered along with the light, but when the wind moves it you see it scattered and gone in every direction. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿like a field of stalks eaten up﴾. He did not suffice with likening them to the stalks until he made it afflicted by the blight [[His saying "bil-akkal" — with a damma, it means the mange/itch (al-hakka). (ʿA)]], nor with likening their deed to the habaʾ until he made it scattered.

Or it is a third object of "ja'alnahu," meaning: We made it combine the insignificance of the habaʾ and its scattering, like His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾, meaning combining the humiliation and the expulsion. The lam of habaʾ is a waw, as evidenced by al-habwa.

Al-mustaqarr (the resting place): the place where they are settled for most of their time, sitting together and conversing.

Al-maqil (the place of midday rest): the place to which they retire to find ease with their spouses and to enjoy flirting with them and touching them, just as the affluent in this world live according to that arrangement. It is related that the reckoning will be concluded in half of that day, so the people of Paradise will take their midday rest in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. In the same sense is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in enjoyment, they and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches﴾ [36:55–56]. It was said in explaining "busy" (shughl): the deflowering of virgins; and there is no sleep in Paradise. He called the place of their leisure and their ease with the houris a "maqil" only by way of metaphor. In the wording "the best" (al-ahsan) there is an allusion to what their place of rest is adorned with: beauty of faces, comeliness of forms, and other embellishments and adornments.

It is also read *tashaqqaqu* (تَشَقَّقُ). The original form was *tatashaqqaqu* (تتشقق). Some readers dropped the second *tā'*, while others assimilated it (*idgham*, the merging of one consonant into the next) into the following letter.

Since the splitting of the sky happens because the clouds come out of it, the clouds are treated as though they are what the sky is split by, as you say: "The hump was split with the blade" (شق السنام بالشفرة) and "it was split by it" (وانشق بها). A parallel is God's words ﴿the sky will be split asunder by it﴾ (السَّماءُ مُنْفَطِرٌ بِهِ).

If you ask what the difference is between saying "the earth split by the plants" (انشقت الأرض بالنبات) and "the earth split open to the plants" (انشقت عن النبات), the answer is this: *inshaqqat bihi* means that God split it by the plants' emergence, so it split by means of them. *Inshaqqat 'anhu* means that the topsoil was lifted away from them when they emerged.

The meaning is that the sky opens up with a cloud coming out of it, and in the cloud the angels descend, with the records of the servants' deeds in their hands. It is also narrated as *tanshaqqu samā'un samā'an* (تنشق سماء سماء), meaning that the heavens split one after another, and the angels descend to the earth.

It was also said that this is a white, thin cloud, like a mist, and that it was given only to the Children of Israel during their wandering (فِي تيههم). Its meaning is similar to God's words ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of cloud, and the angels?﴾ (هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمامِ وَالْمَلائِكَةُ).

It is also read *wa-nunazzilu al-malā'ikata* (وننزل الملائكة), *tanzilu al-malā'ikatu* (وتنزل الملائكة), *nuzzila al-malā'ikatu* (ونزل الملائكة), *nuzzilat al-malā'ikatu* (ونزلت الملائكة), *unzila al-malā'ikatu* (وأنزل الملائكة), *nazzala al-malā'ikata* (ونزل الملائكة), and *nazzala al-malā'ikatu* (ونزل الملائكة). The reading with the omission of the *nūn* (النون), which is the first radical of the verb in *nanzilu*, is the reading of the people of Mecca (أهل مكة).
Al-Haqq: the Established, because every sovereignty will pass away and be annulled on that Day, and only His sovereignty will remain.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verses 27–29:

biting of the hands and fingertips, falling into regret (al-suqut fi al-yad), eating the fingers (akl al-banan), grinding the teeth and molars (harq al-asnan wal-aram), and striking the hands together (qar'uha). These are metonymies (kinayat, figurative expressions) for rage and grief, because they accompany them (min rawadifiha). So he mentions the accompaniment (al-radifa) and thereby indicates what it accompanies (al-mardduf). The speech thus rises to a high level of eloquence, and the listener finds in it a sense of awe and admiration that he does not find in the plain term for what is being alluded to.

[[His statement "wa-harq al-asnan wal-aram" in al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari): "haraqtu al-shay' harqan": I ground it, and I rubbed parts of it against each other. From this comes their saying: "haraqtu nabahu," meaning he crushed it until a grinding sound was heard from it. And "fulan yuharriq 'alayka al-aram ghaydan" (so-and-so grinds his molars at you in rage). Also in it: "arima 'ala al-shay'," meaning he bit down on it, and "aramahu" too, meaning he ate it. And al-aram are the molars, as if it were the plural of ārim. It is said: "fulan yuharriq 'alayka al-aram" when he becomes enraged and grinds his molars against each other. (ع)]]

It was revealed concerning ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams, who used to frequently sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also said that he prepared a feast and invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he refused to eat from his food until he uttered the two testimonies (al-shahadatayn). He did so. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was his friend, so he reproached him and said: "Have you converted, O ʿUqba?" He said: "No, but he swore that he would not eat from my food while he was in my house, so I felt ashamed before him, and I testified for him, though the testimony was not in my heart." Ubayy said: "My face is forbidden to your face if you meet Muhammad and do not step on his neck and spit in his face and slap his eye." He found him prostrating in Dar al-Nadwa and did that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will not meet you outside Mecca without striking your head with the sword." So he was killed on the day of Badr; he ordered ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, to kill him. It is also said that ʿAsim ibn Thabit ibn Aflah al-Ansari killed him, and he said: "O Muhammad, for whom are the captive women (al-sibiyya)?" He said: "For the Fire." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Ubayy at Uhud, and he returned to Mecca and died.

[[Abu Nuʿaym transmitted it in al-Dala'il (Dala'il al-Nubuwwa) through Muhammad ibn Marwan, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, mentioning it at length, but only up to his words: "ʿUqba was taken captive on the day of Badr and killed in cold blood (sabran). No captive was killed on the day of Badr other than him. Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah killed him." Al-Tabari transmitted from Mujahid, regarding Allah's words "And on the day the wrongdoer bites his hands" (25:27), that "ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt invited the Prophet (ﷺ) to a meal he had prepared," up to his words "and I testified for him, though the testimony was not in my heart." And from Muqatil, similarly but abridged, he said: "ʿUqba was killed on the day of Badr in cold blood." As for Ubayy ibn Khalaf, the Prophet (ﷺ) killed him with his own hand on the day of Uhud during the fighting. These are the two whom Allah referred to in "And on the day the wrongdoer bites his hands." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it, and then al-Wahidi, without a chain of transmission.]]

This is also one of their objections and proposals, which show their aversion from the truth and their refusal to follow it. They said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once, in a single time, as the three Books were sent down? And what is wrong with it that it was sent down in parts?" The ones who said this were the Quraysh; it is also said they were the Jews. This is excessive talk and disputation about something of no benefit, because the matter of its inimitability (i'jaz) and the argument from it does not differ whether it is sent down all at once or in parts.

His words "Thus" (kadhalika) are an answer to them, meaning: thus it was sent down in parts. The wisdom in this is: that We strengthen your heart through its division so that you may understand it and memorize it, because the one who is being taught only strengthens his heart to retain knowledge bit by bit, part after part. Had it been cast upon him in one go, he would have been bewildered by it and unable to memorize it [[On his words "lubi'a bihi wa ta'ayya bihafzihi" (he would have been bewildered by it and failed to retain it): in al-Sihah: "ba'ala al-rajul" (with kasra) means he was astonished; and also there: "'ayiytu bi-amri-, idha lam tahtadi li-wajhihi" (I was at a loss in my affair, when I did not find its way), and "a'ya 'alayhi al-amr" and "ta'ayya" and "ta'ayya" have the same meaning. Reflect. (Ga'.)]]. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was different in his situation from the situation of Moses, David and Jesus, peace be upon them, since he was unlettered, unable to read or write, while they were readers and writers. Therefore he had no choice but to receive and memorize, so it was sent down to him gradually over twenty years. It is also said: over twenty-three years.

Also: it used to descend according to events and in answer to questioners, and because some of it abrogates (mansukh) and some of it is abrogating (nasikh), and this could only be done with what was sent down in parts. If you say: the "dhalika" in "kadhalika" must refer to something that preceded it, and what preceded it is its being sent down all at once; so how do you explain it as "thus We sent it down in parts"? I say: because their saying "Why was it not sent down all at once?" means: "Why was it not sent down in parts?"

The proof of the corruption of this objection is that they were unable to produce a single star (najm) of its stars, and they were challenged to produce one single surah of the shortest surahs. They exposed the page of their incapacity and recorded it against themselves, when they took refuge in hostility and resorted to war; then they said: "Why was it not sent down in one go?", as if they could master its parts so that they could master its whole.

"Wa rattalnahu" (and We arranged it) is conjoined to the verb to which "kadhalika" is attached, as if he said: "Thus We divided it and arranged it." The meaning of its tartil (arrangement) is that We made it verse after verse, and pause after pause. It may also be that the meaning is: We commanded the recitation of it to be arranged, and that is His saying: "And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation (tartil)", i.e., read it with deliberateness and steadiness. From this is the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, describing his recitation (ﷺ): "Not like your rapid reciting of this; if a listener wished to count its letters, he could count them." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari, from the transmission of 'Urwa, who said: "Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, sat by the chamber of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, and said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to speak words such that one who counted them could count them." It will come in al-Muzzammil.]] Its original meaning is the tartil of the teeth, which is their being well-spaced and clear: one says "thaghr ratl wa murattal" (a thaghr that is arranged), and it is likened to the light of the chamomile in its spacing. It is also said: it is that We sent it down, even though it was in parts, with deliberation and leisure over a widely spaced period, which is twenty years, and We did not divide it within a closely spaced period.

"And they do not bring you any strange question from their false questions" (this is a figure for falsehood) "but We bring you the true answer which cannot be avoided, and what is better in meaning and in its import than their question." They said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once, in a single time, as the three Books were sent down? And what is wrong with it that it was sent down in parts?" Reflect. (Ga'.)]]. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 37:

Ka-annahum kadhdhabu Nuhan wa-man qablahu min al-rusul sarihan. Aw kana takdhibuhum li-wahid minhum takdhib lil-jami' aw lam yaraw ba'tha al-rusul asla ka-l-Barahima.

Wa-ja'alnahum (wa-ja'alna ighraqahum aw qissatahum) li-l-zalimin. Immā an yu'nā bihim qawm Nuh, wa-asluhu: wa-a'tadna lahum, illa annahu qasada tazlimahum fa-azhar. Wa-immā an yatanawalahum bi-'umumihi.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 38–39:

The word ʿĀdan (ʿĀd) is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "hum" in "jaʿalnāhum" (we made them), or to "al-ẓālimīn" (the wrongdoers), because the meaning is: "And We promised the wrongdoers." It is also read: "Wa-Thamūda" (and Thamūd), according to an interpretation of it as the tribe (al-qabīla). As for the form that takes nunation (al-munṣarif), it is according to an interpretation of it as the living group (al-ḥayy), or because it is the name of the greatest ancestor (al-ab al-akbar).

It was said concerning the People of the Rass (aṣḥāb al-Rass): they were a people among the worshippers of idols, possessors of wells and livestock. So God sent Shuʿayb to them, and he called them to Islam. But they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. While they were around the Rass, which is the unlined well (al-bi'r ghayr al-maṭwiyya), according to Abū ʿUbayda: it collapsed with them, and they were swallowed up, along with their dwellings.

It was also said: al-Rass is a village in Falaj al-Yamāma. They killed their prophet and were destroyed, and they were the remnant of Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ. It was also said: they were the companions of the prophet Ḥanẓala ibn Ṣafwān. They were afflicted by the ʿAnqāʾ, which is the largest of birds, named for the length of its neck, and it used to dwell on their mountain called Fatḥ; it would swoop down on their children and snatch them away when its prey was scarce. Ḥanẓala invoked a curse against it, and a thunderbolt struck it. Then they killed Ḥanẓala, and were destroyed.

It was also said: they were the People of the Ditch (aṣḥāb al-Ukhdūd), and the Rass is the ditch.

It was also said: al-Rass is at Antioch, where they killed Ḥabīb the carpenter (al-najjār).

It was also said: they denied their prophet and threw him into a well (rassūhu fī bi'r), meaning they thrust him into it.

Bayna dhālika (between that): i.e., between that which has been mentioned. The speaker may mention various things and then refer to them with "dhālika," just as the counter may tally numerous figures and then say "that is such-and-such," meaning: that which has been counted or enumerated.

Ḍarabnā lahu al-amthāl (We set forth for them the parables): We explained to them the wondrous stories from the tales of the ancients, and We described to them what they had incurred by denying the prophets and what came upon them of God's punishment and destruction.

Al-tatbīr (ruin): the crushing and breaking into pieces. From it comes al-tibr, which is the fragments of gold, silver and glass.

Kullan (each of them) in the first position is in the accusative, governed by what is indicated by "ḍarabnā lahu al-amthāl," which is: "we warned" (anzarnā), or "we admonished" (ḥadhdharnā). The second is governed by "tabbarnā," because it is left without an object.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 40:

He meant by "the town" Sodom (Sadum), one of the towns of the people of Lut (Lot). There were five of them: God, exalted is He, destroyed four of them along with their inhabitants, and one remained. "Rain of evil" means the stones, meaning that the Quraysh passed many times on their trading journeys to Syria by that town which had been destroyed by stones from the sky. Did they not, in the course of their many passings, look upon the traces of God's punishment and His vengeance, and take heed? Rather, they were a people who disbelieved in the Resurrection, not expecting a rising (nushur) or a consequence ('aqibah). So he placed "hope" (raja') in the place of "expectation" (tawaqqu'), because only one who believes expects a consequence. Therefore they neither looked nor took heed, and they passed by it just as their riding beasts passed by it. Or: they do not hope for a rising as the believers hope for it, out of their desire to reach the reward of their deeds. Or: they do not fear, according to the Tihami dialect.

In (إِنْ) the first is negating, and the second is the lightened form of the heavy (إِنَّ). The lam (اللام) is the one that distinguishes between them. "And takes him in mockery" (واتخذه هزوا):

It means "he mocked him," and the original sense is: he took him as an object of ridicule (موضع هزؤ), or one mocked (مهزوءا به). "Is this he" (أَهذَا) is reported after an implied saying (القول المضمر).

This is belittlement (استصغار), and "God sent forth a messenger" (بَعَثَ اللَّهُ رَسُولًا) is an expression placed in the form of acceptance and affirmation, while they were at the utmost degree of denial and rejection, as mockery and derision. Had they not been mocking, they would have said: "Is this the one who claims or alleges that he has been sent by God as a messenger?" Their saying "He nearly led us astray" (إِنْ كادَ لَيُضِلُّنا) is evidence of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) intense striving in calling them, and his expending of the utmost effort and capacity in winning them over, together with presenting to them the signs and miracles, to the point that, in their own estimation, they were close to abandoning their religion for the religion of Islam, were it not for their extreme obstinacy and their clinging to the worship of their gods. "Had it not been" (لَوْلا) in such speech runs, in meaning, though not in grammatical construction, as a restriction (التقييد) of an absolute ruling. "They will know" (وَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ) is a threat and an indication that they cannot escape it, however long the period of respite lasts, and the threat must certainly reach them, so the delay should not deceive them. His saying "Who is further astray in path?" (مَنْ أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا) is like a reply to their saying "He nearly led us astray," because it attributes to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) misguidance, when none leads astray except one who is himself astray. It is also narrated that it is a saying of Abu Jahl, may God curse him.

Whoever is under the sway of his desire in his religion, following it in everything he does or leaves undone, does not look at any proof nor give ear to any argument. So he is a worshipper of his own desire, and he has made it his god. He says to His Messenger, "This one, who sees no object of worship but his own desire, how can you call him to guidance? Will you rely on him and compel him to Islam, saying, 'He must submit, whether he wills or refuses'—while ﴿there is no compulsion in religion﴾?" This is like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ and ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. It is also related that a man among them would worship a stone, and whenever he saw something better than it, he would cast it aside and take another. Among them was al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi.

Am here is disconnected (*munqati'a*, "disjunctive"). Its meaning is: "Rather, do you suppose that this censure is worse than the one before it, so that the turn is made from that one to this one? This is their being deprived of hearing and understanding, since they do not give an ear to listening to the truth nor a mind to reflecting upon it. They are likened to cattle, which are an example of heedlessness and misguidance, and then they are more astray than cattle."

If you ask why his desire was placed first, when the original would be "he took desire as his god," I say: it is nothing but the fronting of the second object over the first, for concern (*al-'inaya*, "special attention"), as you say, "I knew Zayd to be departing," because of the great concern for the one departing.

[Mahmud said: "If you ask why his god was placed first, though it is the second object, he answered that it was fronted out of concern for it, like your saying, 'I thought departing Zayd,' when your concern is with the one departing." Ahmad said: In this there is a fine subtlety, which is the conveying of exclusivity (*hasr*, "restriction"). The speech before the entry of "have you seen" was a subject and predicate: the subject is "his desire" and the predicate is "his god." The fronting of the predicate, as you know, conveys restriction, so it is as if he said: "Have you seen one who took as his worshipped only his desire?" This is more eloquent in censuring and rebuking him. And God knows best.]

If you ask what is meant by mentioning "most," I say: among them were those whom only one disease prevented from Islam, which is love of leadership, and that is enough of a stubborn disease.

If you ask how they came to be more astray than cattle, I say: because cattle submit to their owners who feed and tend them, and they recognize who does good to them from who does them harm, and they seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them, and they are guided to their pastures and watering places. These people do not submit to their Lord, nor recognize His goodness to them from the evil of Satan, who is their enemy. They do not seek reward, which is the greatest benefit, nor guard against punishment, which is the greatest harm and ruin. And they are not guided to the truth, which is the clear watering place and the sweet, refreshing spring.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verses 45–46:

﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾: Have We not looked at the handiwork and power of your Lord? The meaning of "extending the shadow" (madd al-zill) is that He makes it extend and spread out, so that people benefit from it. ﴿And if He had willed, He would have made it still﴾: that is, adhering to the base of every object that casts a shadow, whether a mountain, a building, or a tree, not spreading out, so that no one benefits from it. He called the spreading and extension of the shadow "movement" (taharruk), and its absence "stillness" (sukun). The meaning of the sun being a "guide" (dalil) is that people are guided by the sun and by its conditions in its course, to know the conditions of the shadow: whether it is fixed in one place, or moving [[The author's phrase "zā'ilan" (moving) is perhaps "zā'ilan 'an ākhar" (moving away from another). (ʿ)]], expanding or contracting. Accordingly, they base their need for the shadow and their independence from it on these conditions. ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us﴾: that He cancels it by the brightness of the sun [[The author's phrase "annahu yansakhuhu bi-ḍaḥḍaḥ al-shams": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "ḍaḥḍaḥa al-sarab" and "taḍaḥḍaḥa" mean that it shimmered; and "al-ḍaḥḥ" means the sun. In a hadith: "None of you should sit between the ḍaḥḥ and the shade, for it is the seat of Satan." (ʿ)]], ﴿gradually﴾: that is, at leisure. In this gradual withdrawal, bit by bit, there are benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated. Had it been withdrawn all at once, most of people's conveniences, through both shade and sunlight, would have been disrupted.

If you ask: where does the particle "thumma" (then) stand in these two places? I say: it indicates the graded superiority of the three matters. The second was greater than the first, and the third greater than both, likening the distance between them in excellence to the distance between events in time.

Another interpretation: He extended the shadow when He built the sky like a stretched dome, and spread out the earth beneath it. The dome cast its shadow upon the earth, a lush shade with no light in it [[The author's phrase "fayyānan mā fī adīmihi jawb": in al-Sihah, "al-fīnān" is the tall one, and "al-adam" is the plural of "adīm" like "afīq" and "afaq", and the surface of the earth is sometimes called "adīm". Also, "jāba yajūbu jawban" means to pierce and cut through, so reflect. (ʿ)]], because there was no light. And if He had willed, He would have made it still, fixed in that state. Then He created the sun and placed it upon that shadow, that is, He set it over the shadow and appointed it as a guide that the shadow follows, as a traveller follows a guide on the road. So the shadow increases and decreases, extends and contracts through it. Then He cancelled it by the sun, withdrawing it with an easy, gradual withdrawal, not a difficult one.

It is also possible that He means: He withdraws it at the Hour (qiyamah) by withdrawing its causes, which are the bodies that sustain the shadow. Thus He mentions its annihilation by the annihilation of its causes, just as He mentioned its creation by the creation of its causes. His words "We have withdrawn it to Us" indicate this, and so does His word "gradually," as He said: ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ (50:44).

﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾: Have We not looked at the handiwork and power of your Lord? The meaning of "extending the shadow" (madd al-zill) is that He makes it extend and spread out, so that people benefit from it. ﴿And if He had willed, He would have made it still﴾: that is, adhering to the base of every object that casts a shadow, whether a mountain, a building, or a tree, not spreading out, so that no one benefits from it. He called the spreading and extension of the shadow "movement" (taharruk), and its absence "stillness" (sukun). The meaning of the sun being a "guide" (dalil) is that people are guided by the sun and by its conditions in its course, to know the conditions of the shadow: whether it is fixed in one place, or moving [[The author's phrase "zā'ilan" (moving) is perhaps "zā'ilan 'an ākhar" (moving away from another). (ʿ)]], expanding or contracting. Accordingly, they base their need for the shadow and their independence from it on these conditions. ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us﴾: that He cancels it by the brightness of the sun [[The author's phrase "annahu yansakhuhu bi-ḍaḥḍaḥ al-shams": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "ḍaḥḍaḥa al-sarab" and "taḍaḥḍaḥa" mean that it shimmered; and "al-ḍaḥḥ" means the sun. In a hadith: "None of you should sit between the ḍaḥḥ and the shade, for it is the seat of Satan." (ʿ)]], ﴿gradually﴾: that is, at leisure. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 47:

He likens what covers the darkness of the night to the enveloping garment. "Al-subat" means death, and "al-masbut" means the dead person, because his life has been cut off. This is like His saying ﴿It is He who takes your souls by night﴾. If you say: why not explain it as rest?

I say: the mention of "al-nushur" (resurrection/rising) in contrast to it rejects that, as a thirsty camel that smells the water and leaves it, while it is muddied (the camel that refuses to drink, shunning muddy water). [[His saying "yaba'uhu iba'a al-'uyuf al-wird wa huwa muranaq" — in al-Sihah, "al-'uyuf" of camels is the one that smells the water and leaves it while thirsty. And there: "raniqtuhu tarniqan": I made it turbid. (Ed.)]]

This verse, along with its indication of the power of the Creator, also shows His blessing upon His creatures, since the concealment by the cover of night contains for many people many religious and worldly benefits. Sleep and waking, and their likeness to death and life, are a lesson in it for whoever takes heed.

And it is reported from Luqman that he said to his son: "My son, just as you sleep and are roused, so you die and are raised."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 48:

It is read as "al-rih" (the wind). "Al-riyah nushran" means "giving life," and "nushran" is the plural of "nushur," which is the one that gives life. "Nushran" is also a lightened form of "nashr," and "bushran" is a lightened form of "bashr," the plural of "bashur" and "bushra." "Wa-bayna yadayi rahmatihi" is a fine metaphor, meaning: in front of the rain. "Tahuran" means extremely pure in its purity. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is what is pure in itself and purifies other things. If what he said is an explanation of its eloquence in purity, it is sound, and it is supported by the words of the Exalted, ﴿and He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾. Otherwise, "fa'ul" is not from the form "taf'il" at all. "Tahur" has two uses in Arabic: as an adjective, and as a non-adjectival noun. The adjectival use is your saying "ma' tahur" (pure water), like your saying "tahir" (pure). The noun use is your saying of what one purifies oneself with: "tahur," like "wudu'" (the water for ablution) and "wuqud" (the fuel) with which one kindles fire. Their saying "tatahhartu tahuran hasanan" (I purified myself with a good purification), like your saying "wudu'an hasanan" (a good ablution), was recorded by Sibawayh. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "There is no prayer except with tahur" [[Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, with "There is no prayer accepted except with tahur." Its origin is in Muslim and al-Tabarani through the route of Isa ibn Sabra from his father from his grandfather, "There is no prayer except with wudu'." There are narrations on this from a group of the Companions. I say: I have fully covered its chains in the beginning of my commentary on al-Tirmidhi, and I mentioned from them only a little.]], meaning purification. If you ask: what removes from water the name "tahur"? I answer: certainty of mixing with impurity, or the assumption that impurity predominates, whether or not one of its three attributes has changed. Or using it on the body to perform an act of worship, according to Abu Hanifa. According to Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both: as long as none of its attributes has changed, it is tahur. If you ask: what do you say about the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked about the well of Buda'a, he said: "Water is tahur; nothing makes it impure except what changes its color, taste, or smell" [[I have not found it in this form. Rather, it is a composite of two hadiths. The first was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan from the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij, who said: O Messenger of Allah, shall we perform ablution from Buda'a, a well into which carrion, dog meat, and filth are thrown? He said: "Water is tahur; nothing makes it impure except what predominates over its color, taste, or smell." I have fully covered its chains in the takhrij of the hadiths of al-Rafi'i.]]? I answer: al-Waqidi said: the well of Buda'a was a channel for water to the gardens.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 49:

He said "dead" (maytan) because "balda" (town/land) carries the sense of "balad," as in His words ﴿So We drove it to a dead land﴾, and because it is not a form that follows the verb pattern, like fa'ul, mif'al and mif'il. It is also read as "nusqiyahu" with a fatha (nasqiyahu). Saqa and asqa are two dialectal forms (lughatan). It is said that asqahu means: he made for him a giving of drink (ja'ala lahu siqyan).

Al-anasi is the plural of insi or insan. Similar to it is zarabi in zaraban, by changing the nun into a ya', and the original is anasin and zarabin. It is also read with lightening by dropping the ya' of the pattern afa'il, as you say "anain" for "anaim" (a'naim).

If you say: sending down water described as pure (tahur), and giving the reason as bringing life and giving drink, indicates that purity is a condition for the validity of that, just as you say: "The emir carried me on a noble horse to hunt wild animals on it." I say:

Since giving drink to the people is among the things for which water was sent down, He described it as pure, honouring them, completing the favour upon them, and clarifying that it is their right, when God wanted purity for them and wanted them to be upon it, that they should prefer it in their inner selves and then in their outer selves, and that they should keep themselves far from mixing with all filth, just as their Lord kept them far from it.

If you say: why did He single out the cattle (al-an'am) from among the animals that drink? I say: because birds and wild beasts go far in seeking water, so drinking does not fail them, unlike cattle. And because they are the possession of the people, and most of their benefits are tied to them, so bestowing on them the giving of drink to their cattle is like bestowing on them the giving of drink to themselves.

If you say: what is the meaning of making "al-an'am" and "al-anasi" indefinite and describing them with abundance? I say: the meaning of that is that most people are settled near valleys, rivers and water sources, so they have no need of rain-water, while their descendants, many of whom are such, are sustained only by what God sends down of His mercy and the watering of His sky. Likewise His words ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ mean some of the lands of these who are far from the places where water is found.

If you say: why did He place the reviving of the earth and the watering of the cattle before the watering of the people? I say: because the life of the people is by the life of their land and their cattle, so He mentioned first what is the cause of their life and subsistence before their drink, and because when they obtain what waters their land and livestock, they will not lack their own drink.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 50:

He means: We have varied this statement among people in the Qur'an and in the other scriptures and pages sent down upon the messengers, peace be upon them, which is the mention of the forming of clouds and the sending down of rain, so that they might reflect and take heed, and recognize the true nature of the blessing therein and give thanks. But most of them refused except ingratitude for the blessing, denying it, and paying no attention to it. It has also been said: We have varied the rain among them in different lands and at different times, and in its differing qualities, from heavy rain and light drizzle, to fine rain and sprinkling, and steady gentle rain and drizzle [[His words "wa-radhdhadh wa-dimma wa-rahham": al-radhdhadh is weak rain; al-rahham is the plural of rahmah, which is a weak, persistent light rain, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]], and they refused except disbelief, and to say: "We have been given rain by such-and-such a star-setting (nawʾ)," and not to mention the making of God and His mercy. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: There is no year with more rain than another year, but God distributes it among His servants as He wills, and he recited this verse [[Recorded by al-Hakim and al-Tabari through the narration of al-Hasan ibn Muslim from Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas. He said: "There is no year with more rain than another year, but God turns it ... etc." On this subject there is also a report from Ibn Masʿud recorded by al-ʿUqaylI through the narration of ʿAli ibn Humayd from Shuʿba, recorded by al-ʿUqaylI through the narration of ʿAli ibn Humayd from Shuʿba from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from him, and he said: it is not followed in its being raised (marfuʿ). Then he recorded it as mawquf through the narration of ʿUmar ibn Marzuq from Shuʿba and said: this is more correct. Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from another route from Ibn Masʿud as marfuʿ.]]. It is also reported that the angels know the number and quantity of the rain each year, because it does not vary, but the lands differ in receiving it.

From here is derived an answer regarding the indefinite forms of "land," "cattle," and "people," as if He said: "That We may give life thereby to some dead lands, and give drink to some of the cattle and people," and that "some" is many. If it is asked: Does one who attributes rain to the star-settings become a disbeliever? I say: If he sees it only as coming from the star-settings and denies that they and the star-settings are both created by God, then he is a disbeliever. But if he holds that God is its creator and has set the star-settings as signs and indicators of it, then he is not a disbeliever.

He says to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have lightened from you the burden of warning all the towns.﴾

﴿And We would have sent into every town a warner.﴾ And We only confined the matter to you and magnified you with it, and honoured you and preferred you over the other messengers. So respond to that with firmness and patience. ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they want from you. He only intends by this to stir him up and to stir up and rouse the believers. The pronoun in ﴿with it﴾ refers to the Qur'an, or to the abandonment of obedience which is indicated by ﴿do not obey﴾. The meaning is: the disbelievers strive and exert themselves to weaken your affair, so respond to them with your own striving and exertion, and with biting down on your molars, by which you overcome and prevail over them. He called it ﴿a great struggle﴾ because of the great hardships it involves.

It is also permissible for the pronoun in ﴿with it﴾ to refer to what is indicated by ﴿And if We had willed, We would have sent into every town a warner﴾, namely his being a warner to all the towns. For if he had been sent to every town as a warner, then every warner would have been obligated to strive against his own town, and all those struggles would have gathered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. His struggle was thereby magnified and made great because of that. So He said to him: ﴿and strive against them with it﴾, by reason of your being a warner to all the towns, ﴿with a great struggle﴾, comprehensive of every kind of struggle.
