Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 53:

He called the two abundant, expansive waters "two seas" (bahrayn), and the sweet one, al-Furat (the extremely sweet, such that it strikes toward sweetness). 

Al-Ajaj is its opposite (the salty, bitter). Their "marj" (mingling/letting loose) means: he left the two of them side by side, adjoining one another, and He, by His power, separates them and prevents them from intermingling. This is among the greatest of His powers. In the words of some of them: "Two seas: one of them alongside the other, mixed (mamruj), and the sweet water of them is with the bitter water, mixed (mamzuj)" [[His saying "mamzuj" is perhaps: "ghayr mamzuj" (not mixed), so let it be verified. (ʿ)]] — a barrier (barzakh), a partition from His power. Like His saying, Most High: ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾, meaning: without visible pillars, and that is His power.

It is read "milh" (on the pattern fa'l). It was said: it is as if it were an elided form of mālih (salty), for lightness, as the poet said: "wa-sulayānan bardan" (and cold marjoram/ṣaliyān), meaning: bāridan (cold).

If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿and a barrier that is forbidding﴾ (ḥijran maḥjūran)?

I say: it is the phrase that the one seeking refuge (al-mutaʿawwidh) says, and we have explained it. Here it is used figuratively, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says to it: "ḥijran maḥjūran," just as His saying ﴿they do not transgress (lā yabghiyān)﴾ means that neither of them transgresses upon the other by mixing. So the absence of transgression there is like seeking refuge here: each of them is made into the form of one who transgresses upon the other, so it seeks refuge from it. This is among the finest metaphors and most evident in eloquence.

Intended meaning: He divided mankind into two kinds, those of lineage (nasab), that is, males to whom descent is traced, so one says "So-and-so son of So-and-so" and "So-and-so daughter of So-and-so"; and those of marriage ties (sihr), that is, females through whom marriage ties are formed. A similar expression is His words, ﴿So He made of him two sexes, the male and the female﴾. ﴿And your Lord is ever Omnipotent﴾, since He created from a single drop of semen two kinds of human beings: male and female.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 55:

"Al-zahir" (helper) and "al-muzahir" (one who backs another) are like "al-ʿawin" (helper) and "al-muʿawin" (one who assists). The form "faʿil" in the sense of "mufaʿil" is not uncommon. The meaning is: the disbeliever backs Satan against his Lord through enmity and polytheism. It is related that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It is also permissible that by "al-zahir" he means the group, as in His saying ﴿and the angels after that are a supporter﴾ [66:4], just as it has come: "al-sadiq" (the friend) and "al-khalit" (the companion), meaning the category. By "the disbeliever" he means the kind, and that some of them back others in extinguishing the light of God's religion. It has also been said: its meaning is: the one who does this deed, which is the worship of what neither benefits nor harms, is against his Lord, insignificant and despised, from the saying of people, "I put him behind my back (zahartu bihi)," when you make him behind your back and do not turn towards him. This is like His saying ﴿They shall have no portion in the Hereafter, nor will God speak to them, nor look at them﴾ [3:77].

An example of ﴿except for whoever wills﴾, meaning: except for the one who does what he wills, and his exception from the reward is like the words of a compassionate person who has worked on your behalf to acquire wealth: "I do not ask you for any reward for what I have striven for, except that you guard this wealth and do not waste it."

So your guarding of your wealth for yourself is not of the category of reward, but he gave it the form of reward and named it by its name. This serves two purposes. The first is to uproot the suspicion of seeking reward from its source, as if he were saying: "If your guarding of your wealth is a reward, then I seek a reward." The second is to show extreme compassion, and that if you guard your wealth, he counts your guarding as a reward and is pleased with it, as one who is rewarded is pleased with a reward. By my life, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was with those sent to them in this regard, and beyond it. The meaning of ﴿taking a way to their Lord﴾ is their drawing near to Him and their seeking nearness to Him through faith and obedience. It has also been said: the meaning is drawing near through charity and spending in the way of God.

He commanded him to place his trust in Him and to entrust his affair to Him for the sufficing of their evil, while holding fast to the foundation of reliance (tawakkul) and its base, which is obedience to Him, worship of Him, glorifying Him (tanzih) and praising Him (tahmid). He informed him that the Living who does not die is worthy of being relied upon alone, and that one should not depend upon any other of the living who die. It is related from some of the early generations (salaf) that he recited it and said: "It is not proper for anyone of sound intellect to place his trust in any created being after this." Then He showed him that He has no part in the affairs of His servants, whether they believe or disbelieve, and that He is All-Aware of their deeds and sufficient as the recompense for their deeds.

Fī sittati ayyāmin, meaning: within a period whose measure is this span (yaʿnī fī muddah), since at that time there was neither day nor night. It was said: six days of the days of the Hereafter, each day being a thousand years. The apparent meaning, however, is that they are days of this world. From Mujāhid: the first of them is Sunday and the last is Friday. Its rationale is that God named those appointed days for His angels with these names; then, when He created the sun and set it in motion and arranged the affairs of the world as they are, the naming applied to these days. As for the reason for this number, namely six rather than other numbers, we have no doubt that it is for a wise purpose (dāʿī ḥikmah), since we know that He does not determine any measure except for a wise purpose, even though we do not perceive it or find our way to knowing it.

Among this is the determination of the angels who are the companions of the Fire as nineteen, the bearers of the Throne as eight, the months as twelve, the heavens as seven and the earth likewise, the prayers as five, and the numbers of the nuṣub (stone idols), the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments), the kaffārāt (expiations), and other things. Affirming the purposes of wisdom in all His acts, and that what He has determined is true and right, is faith.

This has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels, and We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain and those who believed may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾

Then He said: ﴿And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him﴾. This is also the answer as to why He did not create them in an instant, while He is able to do so. From Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with both of them: He created them in six days while He is able to create them in an instant, as a teaching to His creation of gentleness and deliberation. It was also said: their creation was completed on Friday, so Allah made it a festival for the Muslims.

﴿The Most Merciful﴾ (al-Raḥmān) is either the subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿Who﴾ (alladhī khalaqa), or an attribute of the Living (al-Ḥayy), or the predicate of an omitted subject, or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun hidden in ﴿istawā﴾. It was also read as al-Raḥmāni, in the genitive, as an attribute of al-Ḥayy.

It was read fasal, and the bāʾ in bihi is a complement (ṣilah) of sal, as in His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will befall﴾ (saʾala sāʾilun bi-ʿadhābin wāqiʿ), just as it may be ʿan in its complement, as in His saying: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bliss﴾ (thumma latus'alunna yawmaʾidhin ʿani al-naʿīm). So fa-sal bihi is like his saying: "he was concerned with it (ihtamma bihi), cared for it (iʿtanā bihi), occupied himself with it (ishtaghala bihi)." And sa'ala ʿanhu is like your saying: "he investigated it (baḥatha ʿanhu), searched into it (fattasha ʿanhu), inquired into it (naqara ʿanhu)." Or the bāʾ is a complement of khabīran: you make khabīran the object of sal, meaning: ask about Him a man who knows, who will inform you of His mercy; or: ask a man who is expert in Him and His mercy; or: ask, with his questioning, one who is expert, as you say, "I saw a lion by him," meaning by his seeing. The meaning is: if you ask Him, you will find Him All-Aware.

Or you make it a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun (hāʾ), meaning: ask about Him, being knowledgeable of everything.

It was also said: al-Raḥmān is one of the names of Allah mentioned in the earlier Scriptures, and they did not know it, so it was said: ask about this name those among the People of the Book who can inform you, so that one may know who denies it. For this reason they used to say: "We know no Raḥmān except the one in Yamāmah," meaning Musaylima. He was called Raḥmān al-Yamāmah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 60:

"And what is al-Rahman?" It may be a question about the one named by it, since they did not know him by this name, and a question about something unknown is asked with "mā." It may also be a question about its meaning, since it had not been used in their speech, as al-Rahim, al-Rahum and al-Rahim were used. Or, they denied its application to God the Exalted, for ﴿what you command us﴾, meaning: to that which you command us, i.e. to prostrate to it, by analogy with "I commanded you the good" or "for your command to us." It is also read with the letter ya' (yamurrunā, "it commands us"), as if some of them said to others: "Shall we prostrate to what Muhammad (ﷺ) commands us?" Or: "to what the one named al-Rahman commands us, while we do not know what he is." The pronoun in ﴿zādahum﴾ refers to ﴿Prostrate to al-Rahman﴾, because it is the thing that was said.

**al-Burūj** (the zodiacal constellations): the stations of the seven wandering planets: Aries (al-Ḥamal), Taurus (al-Thawr), Gemini (al-Jawzā'), Cancer (al-Saraṭān), Leo (al-Asad), Virgo (al-Sunbula), Libra (al-Mīzān), Scorpio (al-‘Aqrab), Sagittarius (al-Qaws), Capricorn (al-Jadī), Aquarius (al-Dalw), and Pisces (al-Ḥūt). They were called burūj, meaning lofty palaces, because for these planets they are like dwellings for their inhabitants. The word burj is derived from tabarruj (display), because of its visibility.

**Al-sirāj** (the lamp) refers to the sun, as in His saying: ﴿And He made the sun a lamp﴾. It was also read as *surajan* (سرجا), and this means the sun together with the great stars along with it.

al-Ḥasan and al-A‘mash read *wa-qamaran munīran* (وقمرا منيرا). It is the plural of the phrase *laylatun qamrā'* (a moonlit night), as if he had said: *wa-dhā qamarin munīran* (and [a night] possessing a bright moon), because the nights become moonlit by the moon, so he attributed it to them.

A parallel to this, in the survival of the governing word after the omission of the governed word and the substitution of the governed word's place, is the verse of Ḥassān:

*Barada* splashes with the flowing pure wine.

He means: the water of Barada. It is not far-fetched that *qamar* here has the same meaning as *qamar*, like *rushd* and *rushd*, and *‘arab* and *‘arab*.

The khilfah (succession) comes from khalaf, like the rukbah (riding) from rakib: it is the state in which the night and the day succeed one another, each following the other. The meaning is: He made them to be in succession, that is, in alternation: this one follows that one, and that one follows this one.

It is said: "al-layl wa-l-nahar yakhtalifan," just as it is said "ya'taqibani" (they alternate). From it is His saying: ﴿and the alternation of night and dayﴩ (Q. 2:164 and similar). It is also said: "bi-fulan khilfah wa-ikhtilaf," when he frequently goes back and forth to his place of relieving himself (mutabarraz).[[His saying "wa-yuqal bi-fulan khilfah" is perhaps "li-fulan." (Ed.)]] It is read: yadhdhakkaru and yadhdhakkaru.

And on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it is read: yatadhakkaru. The meaning is that an observer should look into their alternation, and so know that their transition from state to state, and their change, requires a mover and a changer. Through this one is to infer the greatness of His power, and the thankful one gives thanks for the blessing in them: the rest at night and the activity by day, as the Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (Q. 28:73). Or [it is said] that they are two periods for those who remember and give thanks: whoever misses, in one of them, his portion of worship and remembrance, makes it up in the other.

And on the authority of al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him:

Whoever's deed of remembrance and thanks is missed during the day, has a chance to make up for it at night. And whoever misses it at night has a chance to make up for it during the day.

And the servants of the Most Merciful (﴿وَعِبَادُ الرَّحْمَٰنِ﴾) is a subject (mubtada', the noun that begins a nominal sentence), whose predicate (khabar) is at the end of the surah. It is as if it were said: "And the servants of the Most Merciful, those whose attributes are these, those are the ones who will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (﴿أُولَٰئِكَ يُجْزَوْنَ الْغُرْفَةَ﴾)." It is also permissible that its predicate is ﴿الَّذِينَ يَمْشُونَ﴾ ("those who walk"). He attributed them to the Most Merciful to single them out and honour them.

It is also recited as "wa-ʿibādu al-Raḥmān" (with the word for servants in the nominative in a different reading). It is recited ﴿يَمْشُونَ هَوْنًا﴾ ("they walk humbly"), where ﴿هَوْنًا﴾ is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), or a description of the walking, meaning "humble ones" (hayyinīn). Or it means "a humble walk," except that placing the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of the adjective is an intensification.

And the proverb:

"If your brother becomes difficult, then be easy (fa-hinn)." Its meaning is: if he is difficult, then be easy and yielding.

The meaning is that they walk with tranquillity, dignity and humility. They do not stamp their feet nor drag their sandals out of arrogance and pride. For this reason some scholars disliked riding in the markets, and because of His saying ﴿وَيَمْشُونَ فِي الْأَسْوَاقِ﴾ ("and they walk in the markets"). 

﴿سَلَامًا﴾ ("peace") means: a greeting of peace from you, not that we are ignorant of you, and a parting with no good and no evil between us. That is, we greet you with a greeting of peace, so the noun "peace" (salām) is placed in the position of the verbal noun "greeting" (taslīm). It was also said: they speak words of rectitude (sadādan) by which they are spared harm and sin. By "ignorance" (al-jahl) is meant foolishness, lack of good manners, and bad piety (sū' al-ruʿa), [[His saying "bad piety" (sū' al-ruʿa): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "So-and-so is bad in piety (sayyi' al-ruʿa)," meaning he has little scrupulousness (warʿ). And in it: it is said that al-wirʿ (with a kasra on the rāʾ) means a pious man. And "warʿa, yaraʿ" (with kasra in both) means ward, wariʿa (scrupulous). (ʿ)]] from his saying:

"Let no one among us act ignorantly against us, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant."

[[The explanation of this line has been given in the second volume, page 390; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

And from Abu al-Aliyah: it was abrogated by the verse of fighting. But there is no need for that, because overlooking fools and refraining from retaliation is commendable in courtesy, manliness and law, and is safer for one's honour and piety.

Al-Baytutah (spending the night): the opposite of al-zulul, which means that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or not. They said: whoever recites any part of the Qur'an in his prayer, even if it is little, has spent the night in prostration and standing. It was also said: they are the two rak'ahs after the maghrib prayer and the two rak'ahs after the 'isha' prayer. The apparent meaning is that it is a description of them as those who enliven the night, or most of it. It is said: so-and-so spends the day fasting and spends the night standing.

**Ghiraman** (ghuraman): destruction, perdition, and ruin, that which is constant and inescapable. He said:

"And the day of al-Nissar and the day of al-Jifar... they were a torment, and they were ghiraman."

This is by Bishr ibn Abi Hazim. Al-Nissar is a water-source of the Banu Amir. Al-Jifar is a water-source of the Banu Tamim in Najd. He means: the battle of al-Nissar and the battle of al-Jifar were a torment upon their people, and they were ghiraman, i.e., inescapable destruction for them. It was also said: constant evil.

And he said:

"If He punishes, it will be ghiraman; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

From the same root is al-gharim (the creditor/debtor who presses for payment), because of his insistence and his binding claim. He described them as those who spend the night in worship, prostrating and standing, then followed this with mention of their supplication, indicating that despite their diligence they are fearful and pleading to God to turn away the punishment from them, as in His saying: "And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful" (23:60). 

**Sa'at** (saa'at) is in the sense of **bi'sa** (an evil/ill term of blame), and in it there is an implicit pronoun that is explained by:

**Mustaqarran** (a place of settling). The object of blame is omitted; its meaning is: "they are evil as a place of settling and a station," with the pronoun referring to it. This pronoun is what links the clause to the subject of **inna** and makes it its predicate.

It is also permissible that **sa'at** means "saddened" (ahzanat). In that case, it contains the pronoun of the subject of **inna**. **Mustaqarran** is then a circumstantial accusative (hal) or a specification (tamyiz). The two explanations may be interwoven and synonymous, and both may be part of God's speech as a quotation of their words.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 67:

It is recited as yaqtarū with the taa' vowelled with a kasra and with a damma. It is also recited as yuqattirū (with the taa' lightened and with it doubled). Al-qatr, al-iqtār and al-taqtīr mean narrowing and restriction, which is the opposite of al-isrāf (extravagance). Al-isrāf is exceeding the limit in spending. Their description is of qaṣd (moderation), which lies between excess (al-ghuluw) and deficiency (al-taqṣīr). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded with the like of this, when God says: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾. It is also said: extravagance is only spending in acts of disobedience; as for spending in acts of devotion, there is no extravagance. A man heard another say: "There is no good in extravagance." He replied: "There is no extravagance in good."

It is related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may God be pleased with him) that he praised ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān when he married him to his daughter and treated him well. He said: "You have joined the ties of kinship, and you have done and made, and you have done." He brought forth fine speech. A son of ʿAbd al-Malik said: "It is only words that he had prepared for this occasion." After some days, he entered upon him while the son was present, and he asked him about his expenses and his circumstances. He said: "The good deed lies between two evil deeds." ʿAbd al-Malik understood that he meant what is in this verse, so he said to his son: "O my son, is this also something he has prepared?"

It is also said: those were the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They would not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty and adornment; rather they would eat what satisfied their hunger and helped them in worshipping their Lord, and wear what covered their nakedness and sheltered them from heat and cold [[His saying "wal-qarr" means cold. (ʿ)]].

ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said: "It is extravagance enough that a man should desire something and then buy it and eat it." [[Al-Thaʿlabī related it. ʿAbd al-Razzāq related it in the Tafsīr from Ibn ʿUyayna from a man from al-Ḥasan from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and this is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) by this route. Aḥmad related it in al-Zuhd from Ismāʿīl from Yūnus from al-Ḥasan likewise. Ibn Māja, Abū Yaʿlā and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab related it by way of Nūḥ ibn Dhakwān from al-Ḥasan from Anas (may God be pleased with him) as a marfūʿ report; the first is more sound.]] 

Al-qawām: justice between two things so that both extremes are upright and balanced. The counterpart of qawām in uprightness is al-sawāʾ from al-istiwāʾ. It is also recited qiwāman (with a kasra), which means that by which a thing is sustained. It is said: "You are our qiwām," meaning what sustains the need, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. As for the two accusatives, "bayna dhālika qawāman": it is permissible for both to be predicates together; or for bayna dhālika to be treated as superfluous (laghw) and qawāman as a stable predicate; or for the adverbial phrase to be the predicate and qawāman an emphatic circumstantial (ḥāl). Al-Farrāʾ permitted that bayna dhālika be the subject of kāna, being indeclinable because it is attached to a non-declinable noun, as in the verse:

"Drinking from it was not prevented, except that it spoke."

[[The explanation of this line was given earlier in the second volume, page 422, so refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector)]]

Grammatically this is not objectionable, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a qawām, so the predicate, which is the principal point of benefit, carries no benefit.

God forbade it—that is, forbade them. The meaning is: He forbade their killing. And "except by right" is connected to this omitted killing.

Al-athām, like al-wabāl, is the requital of sin. It has been said that it is the sin itself, so the thing is named after its cause, namely the requital. The second object of jazā is omitted. And "al-'uqūq" is the subject, meaning: the disobedience must have a terrible, great requital.]]

It has also been said that athām is the sin itself, and its meaning is: he will meet the requital of sin. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read: ayyāman (ayyāman), meaning hardships. It is said: "a day that is dhū ayyām," for a grievous day. Yuḍā'af (yuḍā'af) is a substitute for yalqa, since both have one meaning, like his saying:

"Whenever you come to us in our abodes, you will find firewood, substantial, and a blazing fire."

It was also read: yuḍa'if, and nuḍa'if lahu al-'adhāb (nuḍa'if lahu al-'adhāb), with the nūn and the accusative al-'adhāb. It was also read with the nominative, as a resumption or as a circumstantial clause; likewise yakhlud. It was also read: wa-yakhlud (wa-yakhlud), in the passive, lightened and intensified, from ikhlād and takhlīd. It was also read: wa-takhlud, with the tā' by iltifāt. Yubaddilu is lightened and intensified, and likewise sayyi'ātihim. If you ask: what is the meaning of doubling the punishment and changing evil deeds into good deeds? I say: when the polytheist commits sins along with polytheism, he is punished for the polytheism and for the sins together, so the punishment is doubled because the thing punished for is doubled. As for changing evil deeds into good deeds: He erases them through repentance and establishes good deeds in their place: faith, obedience, and piety. It has also been said: He changes for them polytheism into faith, the killing of Muslims into the killing of polytheists, and fornication into chastity and marriage-protection.

It is as if he says: whoever abandons the sins, repents of them, and enters into righteous deeds, then by that he is one who turns in repentance to God with a repentance (matāban) that is pleasing to Him, expiating sins and securing reward. Or: "then indeed he turns in repentance to God," i.e., one who turns back to God (mutāban mutāban ilā Allāh), the One who knows the right of those who repent and does to them what they deserve; and He loves those who turn much in repentance and loves those who purify themselves. In the speech of some Arabs: "God is more pleased with the repentance of a servant than with the one who has lost his mount and found it, the thirsty one who reaches water, and the barren one who bears a child." Or: "then he returns to God and to His reward with a good return, and what a return!"

It may be that they turn away from the gatherings of liars and the assemblies of sinners, so they neither attend them nor draw near to them, keeping themselves pure from mixing with evil and its people, and preserving their religion from what would diminish it, for the presence at scenes of falsehood is a form of partnership in it. For this reason it has been said concerning those who look on at everything the Sharia does not permit: "They are partners of its doers in the sin," because their attendance and their looking are a sign of approval of it and a cause of its existence and its increase, since what drove the doing of it is the admiration of the onlookers and their desire to watch it. And in the admonitions of Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon him, it is said: "Beware of sitting with sinners."

It may also be that they do not give false testimony (shahadat al-zur), in which case the genitive noun has been omitted and the noun in the genitive has been put in its place.

Qatadah said: "The gatherings of falsehood." Ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: "Frivolity and singing." Mujahid said: "The festivals of the polytheists."

Al-laghw (vain talk, frivolity): everything that ought to be discarded and cast aside. The meaning is: when they pass by people of vain talk and those who busy themselves with it, they pass by turning away from them, honoring themselves by not stopping among them or plunging in with them, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾ On the authority of al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him: "Sins did not make them foolish."

It was also said: when they hear from the disbelievers insults and harm, they turn away and forgive. And it was said: when they mention marriage (al-nikah), they refer to it by allusion.

﴿They do not fall down upon them﴾ is not a negation of falling down. It is an affirmation of it, and a negation of deafness and blindness, just as you say: "Zayd does not meet me greeting me (لا يلقاني زيد مسلما)." The negation applies to the greeting, not to the meeting.

The meaning is this: when they are reminded of these signs, they bend over them eagerly to listen, and they turn toward the one who reminds them. While they are bent over them, they listen with attentive ears and look with watchful eyes. This is unlike those who are reminded by them and yet are seen bending over them and turning toward the one who reminds them, showing intense eagerness to listen, while they are like the deaf and blind, not comprehending them and not perceiving what is in them, like the hypocrites and their likes.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 74:

It is read: "dhurriyyatina" (dhurriyyatina) and "dhurriyyatina" (dhurriyyatina); and "qurrata a'yun" and "qurrat a'yun." They asked their Lord to grant them spouses and descendants who are obedient to Allah, who gladden them by their station, and whose eyes are gladdened by their drawing near. And on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ka'b: There is nothing more delightful to the eye of the believer than to see his wife and his children obedient to Allah. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: it is the child when he sees him writing jurisprudence (fiqh). It has also been said: they asked that Allah join their spouses and descendants to them in Paradise, so that their joy might be complete. He intended "a'immah" (imams), and was content with the singular because it indicates the category and because there is no ambiguity, as in His saying, "Then He brings you out as a child" (Qur'an 22:5). Or they meant: make each one of us an imam. Or "a'imma" is the plural of "amm" (one who leads), like "sa'im" and "siyam." Or they meant: make us a single imam, owing to our unity and the harmony of our word. It was also said by some of them: the verse indicates that leadership in religion should be sought and desired. It has also been said: these verses were revealed concerning the ten who were given the glad tidings of Paradise.

If you ask: what is "min" in His saying "min azwajina"? I say: it may be explicative (bayaniyyah), as if it were said: "Grant us the coolness of eyes," then the coolness is specified and explained by His saying "from our spouses and our descendants." Its meaning is: that Allah makes them a coolness of eyes for them, and this is from their saying, "I saw from you a lion," meaning, "you are a lion." And it may be initial (ibtida'iyyah), in the sense of: "Grant us, from their side, what will delight our eyes through obedience and righteousness."

If you ask: why did He say "qurrata a'yun" indefinitely and in a small number? I say: as for the indefiniteness, it is for the sake of the indefiniteness of "qurrah," since an annexed noun (mudaf) cannot be made indefinite except by making the noun it is annexed to indefinite; as if it were said: "Grant us from them joy and gladness." And "a'yun" was said rather than "uyun" because he intended the eyes of the God-fearing, and these are few in comparison with the eyes of others. Allah the Exalted said, "And few of My servants are grateful" (Qur'an 34:13).

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: why did He use 'a'yun' (the paucity form) when 'a'yun' is the form of the plural of paucity? I say: because the eyes of the God-fearing are few in comparison with others, as is indicated by His saying, 'And few of My servants are grateful.'" Ahmad said: The apparent meaning is that what is related is the speech of each one of the God-fearing, so it is as if he said: each one of them says, "Make for us from our spouses and descendants a coolness of eyes." This is safer than his interpretation, for although the God-fearing are few in comparison with others, they are in themselves numerous. What is taken into account in applying the plural of paucity is that the group itself be few in itself, not by relation and comparison. And Allah knows best.]]

It is also permissible to say, regarding the indefiniteness of "a'yun," that they are a specific kind of eyes, namely the eyes of the God-fearing.

What is meant is that they will be rewarded with the chambers (al-ghurafat), which are the upper halls in Paradise. He used the singular form, which denotes the category, and the evidence for this is His saying ﴿and they will dwell secure in the chambers﴾ and the reading of the one who read: في الغرفة (fi al-ghurfa). "For what they endured" means for their patience in obedience, in abstaining from desires, in bearing the harm of the disbelievers and striving against them, and in enduring poverty and other things.

The unrestricted form of the word is for the sake of generality, covering every matter endured. It was also read: يلقون (yulaqqawn), as in His saying ﴿and He gave them radiance and joy﴾, and يلقون (yalqa), as in His saying ﴿and he will meet a penalty﴾. "Tahiyya" is a prayer for long life, and "salam" is a prayer for safety. That is, the angels greet them and offer them the salutation of peace. Or some of them greet one another and salute one another. Or they are given enduring continuance and eternity together with safety from every calamity. O Allah, grant us success in obeying You, make us among the people of Your mercy, and provide us with what You provide them in the abode of Your good pleasure.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 25, verse 77:

When He described the worship of His servants, enumerated their righteous deeds and good works, praised them for these, and promised them an elevation in rank in Paradise, He followed this with an explanation that He cares for those people, gives weight to them, raises their mention, and promises them what He promises them, only because of their worship. So He commanded His Messenger to declare to the people, and to state firmly to them, that the regard in which they are held by their Lord is for worship alone and for no other reason. Had it not been for their worship, He would not have cared for them at all, nor counted them, nor would they have been anything of consequence to Him. *Al-du'a'* (supplication) means *al-ibadah* (worship). *Ma* here contains the meaning of interrogation and is in the accusative position, and it refers to the verbal noun, as if it were said: "What weight would your Lord give you, were it not for your supplication?" The meaning is that you do not deserve any weight from Him were it not for your worship. The literal sense of their saying *ma 'abata bihi* is: "I counted it among the heavy burdens of my concerns and among what is a burden upon me," just as you say *ma iktaratu lahu*, meaning: "I counted it among my calamities and among what concerns me." Al-Zajjaj said, in interpreting ﴿ما يعبأ بكم ربي﴾: "What weight would you have in His sight?"

It is also permissible for *ma* to be negative. Then the meaning of ﴿فقد كذبتم﴾ is: "When I have informed you that My judgment is that I count My servants only for their worship, you have opposed My judgment by your denial, so there will certainly befall you the consequence of your denial, until it casts you into the Fire."

A parallel to this in speech is when a king says to one who has disobeyed him: "It is my custom to show kindness to whoever obeys me and follows my command. You have disobeyed, so you will see what will befall you because of your disobedience." It has also been said that the meaning is: "What would your Lord do with you were it not for His calling you to Islam?" And it has been said: "What would He do with your punishment were it not for your invoking others alongside Him as gods?" If you ask: "To whom is this address directed?" I say: to people in general, among whom are believing worshippers and deniers who disobey. They are addressed with what is found in their kind, of worship and denial.

It is recited: ﴿فقد كذب الكافرون﴾. It has also been said that the punishment will be ﴿لزاما﴾ (inevitable). It is narrated from Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, that it refers to the killing on the day of Badr, and that it was made to cling to the slain (*lazima bayn al-qatla lizaman*). It is also recited *lizaman* with a fatha, in the sense of *al-luzum* (adherence), like *al-thabat* and *al-thubut* (both meaning firmness).

The preferable view is that the subject of *kana* is left unspoken after it has been known that it is among what is threatened, for the sake of ambiguity and to encompass what description cannot grasp. And Allah knows best what is correct.
